sowhat: For sixty years the systems we depend on, the water plant, the power grid, the 911 center, the hospital down the road, have been engineered against accidents: storms, floods, a pump that fails, an operator who makes a mistake. They are engineered well. But the whole discipline rests on an assumption nobody ever had to write down, that whatever comes at you is indifferent to your defenses. A flood does not wait for the night shift. A storm does not come back for the repair crew.

A deliberate adversary does. It chooses its moment, it keeps coming, it aims at the one point that matters, and it blocks the repair. Those four things, intentionality, persistence, precision and denial, are what this work adds to the design basis. And because these systems lean on one another, losing one is rarely the end of it: the hospital needs the water, the water needs the power, and the power needs the phones. Every real event on this site is a case where that happened, most of them without any adversary at all.

The point is not alarm. It is that what we can describe, we can design for. A design basis is a written promise of exactly what a facility must withstand, made in advance and on the record, so that anyone can check it and everyone knows when it has been exceeded. This site shows one example of that promise for each sector: what we postulate, what actually happened, and where the design holds and where it hands off to someone else.

intro: Every facility on this site is built to do something. A water system delivers water, a power plant generates power, a 911 center answers calls. That job is its function. Safety is not the function; it is a requirement on how the function is done. Nothing is built simply to be safe. It is built to do something, and it must do that thing safely.

A design basis is the written promise of what the facility must withstand while it does its job, and what counts as success when it is tested. This work writes that promise in three layers, each building on the one before.
body: **The design basis** names the function, the people, process and technology that deliver it, and the limits within which it is done. Success is simple: the function is delivered within those limits.

**The design basis accident** adds the events experience has taught us to expect: fire, flood, storm, a failed component, an operator's error, a process flaw nobody anticipated. These are bounded because experience is bounded. Success means the facility either keeps working or reaches a safe, known condition, and then recovers with the help of the outside world: off-site power, repair crews, supplies, emergency services.

That second layer quietly assumes three things. Events are indifferent to how the facility responds. Each event runs its course and ends. And outside help remains available. **Deliberate military action**, the third layer, is defined by an adversary who removes those assumptions. It chooses the moment and adapts (intentionality). It keeps coming (persistence). It aims at the parts whose loss is hardest to recover from (precision). And it blocks repair and outside help (denial). An actor counts as this kind of adversary by what it can do, not by who it is.

So success changes. Recovery can no longer be counted on, because the adversary can defeat it. The facility must instead reach and hold a protected state, keeping the harm bounded, using only what is at the facility, for as long as the attack lasts. It may stop doing its job. It never stops doing it safely.

Two things move in opposite directions as you go from left to right in the picture. The conditions a design must withstand widen, and so the designs that meet them narrow. And everything rests on a single function held constant through all three layers, which is what makes them one progression rather than three separate analyses.

The real events on this site run the other way. A reference event reads something that actually happened back through the design basis and asks whether the method was enough. What it finds goes back to revise the design basis. Most of those events involved no adversary at all, and that is part of the lesson: a design that cannot survive the accident will not survive the attack.

request: The site shows one example for each sector and a summary card for each use case. Fuller material exists: the full use cases, the other facility classes marked as written, and more detailed versions of the documents shown here.

That material is released to defenders, regulators and researchers on request. Each request is read by the author, each release is vetted, and released material is marked under the Traffic Light Protocol, which tells the recipient how far it may be shared.

To ask, send a private message to the author through timroxey.substack.com. Please use a private message rather than a public comment, say who you are and what you work on, and name the sector and the documents you are asking about. A public comment is the wrong place to ask for marked material.
Nothing on this site is regulatory guidance or a compliance checklist.
master_draft: The master draft applies the design basis approach to governing generative AI in critical infrastructure control. Several of its chapters read the examples on this site, and each sector page that has one points to the chapter that reads it.
